summary: A 1977 Telnet option for data entry terminals. It was replaced by RFC 732.

eli5.summary: Some old terminals worked like forms to fill in. This option lets a computer handle them correctly.

subtitle: A Telnet option for data entry form terminals

tldr.problem: Data entry terminals that display forms need a way to handle special features like field protection, cursor positioning, and selective screen areas through Telnet.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 731 defines a Telnet option using subnegotiation commands to control cursor movement, editing, erasing, formatting and data transmission, with negotiation of terminal capabilities.
tldr.outcome: This early approach was replaced by RFC 732 with an improved design.

facts.label: Minimal implementation
facts.value: 9 core subcommands plus line/page size negotiation

facts.label: Cursor topology
facts.value: Finite plane or toroidal, absolute or relative

today: RFC 731 is Historic, having been replaced by RFC 732 the same year.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal
sections.content:
RFC 731 specifies a Telnet option for Data Entry Terminals (DET) designed to support form-based terminals through a Network Virtual Data Entry Terminal (NVDET). Unlike traditional scroll-mode terminals, data entry terminals display formatted information on a rectangular screen where fields can be protected, highlighted, or restricted to specific input types.

The RFC was created because Telnet, originally designed for simple teletypes, could not handle the features these terminals needed: cursor positioning anywhere on the screen, field protection, intensity control, and the ability to transmit only certain portions of the display. Instead of encoding these controls as ASCII characters, the DET option uses Telnet subnegotiation commands to keep all control information out of the data stream, preserving transparency.
sections.eli5: The option lets a computer handle form terminals by sending special control commands through Telnet. It can move the cursor, protect fields from editing, and control what parts of the screen get sent back.

sections.title: Capabilities and Facilities
sections.content:
The DET option defines five classes of functions: facility negotiation, editing operations, erasure operations, formatting, and transmission control. Implementation begins with facility negotiation, where hosts exchange capability maps describing what features they support: toroidal cursor addressing, line and character insertion/deletion, field protection, blinking, reverse video, intensity levels, and other attributes.

A minimal implementation must support cursor movement, home, erase screen, transmit screen, format data, and error reporting. More sophisticated implementations can negotiate additional features like back-tab, protection suppression, and character-level repeat compression. The protocol allows implementations to learn about terminal capabilities dynamically rather than requiring them at connection start.
sections.eli5: Before doing anything fancy, the two ends agree on what features they both support. Then the server can use those features to control the display.

sections.title: Screen Control and Data Transmission
sections.content:
The DET option provides editing commands for cursor control: absolute positioning (MOVE CURSOR), toroidal wrapping (SKIP TO LINE, SKIP TO CHAR), and directional movement (UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT). Other editing functions include HOME, line and character insertion/deletion, and the ability to read the current cursor position.

Formatting commands apply attributes to screen regions: blinking, reverse video, right justification, protection levels, and intensity. Transmission commands let the server request specific data: TRANSMIT SCREEN sends everything, TRANSMIT UNPROTECTED sends only unprotected fields, and TRANSMIT FIELD or TRANSMIT LINE send specific areas. The server sends a DATA TRANSMIT command before data to indicate the starting cursor position, allowing intelligent implementations to avoid re-sending unchanged areas.
sections.eli5: The server sends commands to move the cursor, mark fields as protected, apply special display effects, and ask for the user's input from specific parts of the screen.

sections.title: Legacy Status
sections.content:
RFC 731 defined an ambitious approach to form-based terminal support through Telnet. However, the overhead of encoding terminal functions as Telnet subnegotiations proved problematic: a single-byte operation in real terminals required up to six bytes in the DET option. The RFC acknowledges this in an appendix discussing the Byte Macro Option to compress frequently used commands.

RFC 732, published the same year, superseded this specification with a revised design. The general approach of using Telnet options to abstract different terminal types remained influential, but implementations of the original DET option were limited.
sections.eli5: This approach had overhead problems and was replaced by RFC 732 with a better design.

items.title: Facility Negotiation
items.text: Hosts exchange capability maps for editing, erasing, formatting, and transmission features.

items.title: Cursor Control
items.text: Absolute and relative positioning, wrapped or bounded, home to (0,0), and position reporting.

items.title: Field Protection
items.text: Mark areas as protected, alphabetic-only, numeric-only, with intensity and blinking attributes.

items.title: Data Management
items.text: Selective transmission of screen, unprotected fields, lines, or regions with optional compression.
